titleText.es: Esa camiseta te sienta bien, pero estaría aún mejor metida en el cuello de una botella de vodka y lanzada en llamas por la ventana de nuestro de edificio de oficinas. Hagámoslo de una puta vez y no miremos atrás.
titleText.en: That shirt looks good on you, but it would look even better stuffed into the neck of a vodka bottle and thrown flaming through the window of our office building. Let's fucking do it once and for all and not look back.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish source contains the wording “nuestro de edificio”; it is preserved exactly above rather than silently corrected.

regions.labelEs: SI PUDIERA REORDENAR EL ALFABETO, ME PONDRÍA JUNTO A TU HERMANA.

applications.exampleEs: SI PUDIERA REORDENAR EL ALFABETO, ME PONDRÍA
applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the imagined condition, pudiera gives the hypothetical ability, and pondría gives the result as what the speaker would do.
Junto a forms one location expression introducing the person placed beside the speaker.
The irregular stem pondr- comes from poner, and the ending -ía marks what the speaker would do.

regions.labelEs: ¿TU PADRE ES UN LADRÓN? PORQUE LO QUE HAS APARCADO FUERA ES MI VOLKSWAGEN.

applications.explanationEn: Porque is written as one unaccented word because it supplies a reason; it does not ask “why?”
Lo que introduces an unnamed thing—the thing that the listener parked—without repeating a noun.
Has identifies informal singular “you,” and aparcado names the completed parking action.

regions.labelEs: DEBES DE ESTAR CANSADA, PORQUE HAS ESTADO CORRIENDO POR MI MENTE DURANTE TODA LA NOCHE.

applications.explanationEn: Debes de introduces an inference about the listener, and estar remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Cansada ends in -a because the speaker describes a woman; cansado would describe a man.
Porque is written as one unaccented word because it introduces the reason for the inference.
Has identifies informal singular “you,” estado supplies “been,” and corriendo presents running as an ongoing activity.
Corriendo por mi mente uses physical movement as a metaphor for repeatedly occupying the speaker's thoughts.
Toda and la both use feminine singular forms to match noche, and together the phrase means the entire night.
The isolated -ando form adds how the previously mentioned running was happening: while screaming.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe an imagined “if…, …would…” situation?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a hypothetical past verb form for the condition, and use a “would” form for the result.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls the condition's verb form the imperfect subjunctive. It often ends in -ra or -se, as in tuviera or tuviese. The result uses the conditional, often ending in -ría, as in haría. In this pattern, do not put the conditional directly after si.

example.en: If I had time, I would travel more.

cards.answerEn: I could; if I were able to
cards.noteEn: Pudiera is a hypothetical form of poder, “to be able to.” After si, it presents the ability as imagined rather than real.

example.es: Si pudiera elegir, viajaría en tren.
example.en: If I could choose, I would travel by train.

cards.answerEn: to rearrange; to put in a new order

cards.promptEs: reordenar el alfabeto · junto a tu hermana
cards.answerEn: a twist on the familiar alphabet pickup line about putting “U and I” together
cards.noteEn: The stock English line uses the letter names U and I as the words “you” and “I.” This joke breaks the expected romantic ending by choosing the listener's sister instead.

cards.answerEn: myself; marks the speaker in a reflexive verb
I would put; I would place
cards.noteEn: Pondría is the conditional form of poner for the speaker. The ending -ía supplies the “would” meaning, while pondr- is the irregular conditional stem.

example.es: Yo pondría la mesa junto a la ventana.
example.en: I would put the table next to the window.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.answerEn: next to; beside (as part of junto a)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one person or thing is next to another?
cards.answerEn: Use junto a before the person or thing that is beside it.
cards.noteEn: Junto a is a fixed location expression meaning “next to” or “beside,” so junto stays unchanged inside it: la farmacia está junto a la estación. The adjective junto, junta, juntos, or juntas is a different construction, as in Ana y Marta están juntas.

example.es: La farmacia está junto a la estación.
example.en: The pharmacy is next to the station.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes junto a, “next to”

cards.noteEn: Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Aparcado is the completed-action form of aparcar, “to park.” It follows a form of haber in a completed-action construction.

example.es: He aparcado cerca de la estación.
example.en: I have parked near the station.

cards.noteEn: Debes is a form of deber for informal singular “you.” In deber de followed by an action verb, it expresses an inference about what is probably true rather than a duty.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something must be true because the evidence makes it likely?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern makes an inference or educated guess. Without de, deber plus an action verb more often expresses a duty or what someone should do.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks an inference after deber
cards.noteEn: In deber de plus an action verb, de helps mark a guess or conclusion about what is likely true.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has been doing an activity over a period of time?
cards.answerEn: Use a present form of haber, then estado, then the activity verb in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: Only the form of haber changes for the person: he for “I,” has for informal “you,” ha for “he,” “she,” or formal “you,” and so on. Estado and the final -ando/-iendo form stay unchanged. That last form presents the activity as ongoing.

example.es: He estado leyendo toda la tarde.
example.en: I have been reading all afternoon.

cards.noteEn: Estado is the completed-action form of estar, the verb for being or being in a state. After a helper such as he, has, or ha, it supplies the idea “been” and does not change for the person.
Corriendo is the ongoing-action form of correr. It ends in -iendo and stays unchanged after estado.

example.es: Han estado corriendo por el parque.
example.en: They have been running through the park.

cards.promptEs: correr/pasar por la mente de alguien
cards.questionEn: How do you say that a thought goes through someone's mind?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of correr or pasar, then por, then the person's mente.
cards.noteEn: The expression treats a thought as moving through the mind. A possessive can identify the person: por mi mente, por tu mente, or por su mente.

example.es: La idea pasó por mi mente.

cards.answerEn: through; around (in correr por la mente)

cards.promptEs: todo/toda + el/la + período de tiempo singular
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something continues for an entire day, night, week, or similar period?
cards.answerEn: Use todo or toda, then the matching singular article el or la, then the time period.
cards.noteEn: Todo and the article match the time noun: todo el día, toda la noche, toda la semana. This pattern covers the whole named period. Plural forms such as todos los años usually mean “every year” and are a separate frequency pattern.
Gritando is the ongoing-action form of gritar. When it appears on its own after another action, it can add how that action was happening.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.
